newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori seizes initiative in hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori seizes initiative in hostage crisis.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori seized the initiative on Wednesday in an increasingly fierce propaganda war with publicity-conscious Marxist guerrillas holding 74 hostages in Lima.

With no concrete developments in the deadlocked crisis since New Year's Day, a relaxed and joking Fujimori led an election-style tour through Lima's poor neighbourhoods to prove the rebel siege had not paralysed the country.

"This is a great demonstration ... in favour of the government, in favour of peace, and against violence," said Fujimori, clad in jeans and a white casual shirt as he headed a caravan of hundreds of journalists and officials.

The visit, which followed a previous tour on Tuesday to shanty-towns and a prison holding some Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, contrasted starkly with Fujimori's previous wall of silence and grim expression during his few public appearances since the crisis began.
To cries of "We are with you" from the crowds who came out to greet him, Fujimori again lambasted as "terrorists" the MRTA rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's residence for 22 days.
"There is no MRTA follower here," Fujimori said. "You have suffered violence ... We are not going to allow the terrorists to continue killing."

He promised to remain "firm" against the MRTA's demand to release all its roughly 400 jailed comrades and urged Japanese companies not to give in to demands for ransoms for their representatives inside the residence.
Although the MRTA has in the past kidnapped businessmen and politicians to raise money, there has been no evidence that this was their aim in the current crisis.
Underscoring the government's new propaganda offensive, diplomats abroad and public relations officials in Peru were told to begin damage-limitation publicity campaigns.

"Much of the news coverage paints the MRTA as if they were good boys, idealistic and romantic, when in fact they are terrorists, and that's how the Peruvian people regard them," said one Peruvian diplomat in another Latin American capital during a briefing with journalists.

"Anybody who grew up in Latin America in the 1960s or 1970s saw (Cuban revolutionary) Che Guevara as this romantic, heroic figure, fighting for the poor and all. But these people aren't like that at all."

Beatriz Boza, head of the government's public relations unit Promperu, told reporters that despite the crisis, Peru had received a total $1.5 billion in foreign investment and loans since the Dec. 17 takeover.

In Vancouver, British Columbia, parliamentarians from 25 Pacific Rim countries on Wednesday called on Peruvian rebels to release the hostages and urged the Peruvian government "not to bargain with terrorists."

Until Wednesday, the MRTA had been overshadowing the government with a slick propaganda campaign ranging from the crude tactics of cardboard placards and megaphones to daily updating of Internet pages and an international spokesman on call in Germany.

As well as abandoning its previous silence, the government also took a tougher approach on Wednesday to journalists covering the crisis, detaining a reporter and a translator working for Japan's TV Asahi. The pair sneaked past police on Tuesday for a two-hour meeting with the MRTA.
Peruvian anti-terrorism police confiscated the pair's notebooks and cameras and said they would be held for at least five days while authorities decide whether to press charges.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi both condemned the pair's action as likely to jeopardise efforts to solve the crisis.
The rebels sought to turn the controversy over TV Asahi to their advantage on Wednesday, showing a placard that read: "Now journalists are arrested to hide the truth."
The MRTA rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took about 500 hostages including ambassadors and senior Peruvian government officials. Most of them were later released.
The guerrillas have said they will stay in the residence as long as necessary to secure the release of their comrades.
In an interview with CNN on Wednesday prior to his tour, Fujimori said: "We are waiting for a favourable condition for beginning again the talks" with the MRTA.

Fujimori also ruled out considering peace talks with the MRTA after or during the hostage crisis, and added that he would not use force against the hostage-takers as long as the captives were not hurt, according to CNN.
